name: Kiwifruit
summary: Very rich in vitamin C, and one of the best-tested foods for constipation: two kiwifruit a day eased it as well as psyllium fibre, or slightly better. In small trials it also lowered blood pressure a little.

lore.who: Zhou-dynasty China (the Book of Songs, Shijing, about 1000–600 BC)
lore.belief: In the song 'In the lowlands grows the chang chu', the singer looks at a supple, glossy vine in flower and in fruit and envies it: 'I delight that you know nothing… that you have no family… that you have no household.' The 12th-century scholar Zhu Xi read it as the lament of people worn down by harsh rule and heavy taxes, who wished they were plants, with no knowledge and no worries.
lore.note: Commentators named the chang chu as the yangtao, a vine whose fruit is 'also like a peach', and a 2022 review says the kiwifruit's genus, Actinidia, was first recorded in the Book of Songs. That identification was made long after the song, so it isn't certain. The song is about envying a carefree plant, not about eating its fruit.

lore.who: Tang-dynasty China (the poet Cen Shen, 8th century)
lore.belief: Visiting an old farmer by the East Creek below Mount Taibai, known far and near to be a hundred years old, with children and grandchildren already grey-haired, Cen Shen wrote that in the middle of the courtyard, over the railing of the well, grew 'a trellis of mihoutao'. The vine was part of a simple country life that made him say he only now saw how wearing the world was.
lore.note: The poem doesn't say the fruit gave the old man his long life. It shows the vine grown beside a farmhouse more than a thousand years before kiwifruit became an orchard crop.

sources.title: Written at old Zhang's house by the East Creek below Mount Taibai, sent to my younger brothers and nephews (in Chinese; Complete Tang Poems, chapter 198)
sources.author: Cen Shen

lore.who: China (the herbalists Chen Cangqi, Tang dynasty, and Kou Zongshi, Song dynasty, as quoted by Li Shizhen)
lore.belief: Mihoutao was a 'cold' fruit, sour and sweet. Chen Cangqi warned that eating a lot of it chills the spleen and stomach and loosens the bowels. Kou Zongshi said it suited people with 'excess heat', and that too much of it makes the organs cold and brings on diarrhoea.
lore.note: 'Cold' and 'heat' belong to Chinese medicine's own theory, which studies don't measure. The part about the bowels fits what trials found: two green kiwifruit a day gave somewhat more bowel movements, with few side effects. No trial has tested eating large amounts.

sources.author: Li Shizhen

lore.who: Ming-dynasty China (Li Shizhen, Compendium of Materia Medica, Bencao Gangmu, 1578)
lore.belief: Li Shizhen explained the names: the fruit is shaped like a pear and coloured like a peach, and macaques love to eat it, so it was called mihoutao, 'macaque peach', and mihouli, 'macaque pear'; people in Fujian called it yangtao. The older herbalists he quoted said the brown, egg-sized fruit turns sweet only after the frost, and that it was left only on low hills beside the roads, because deep in the mountains the monkeys ate most of it.
lore.note: Mihoutao is still the Chinese name generally used for kiwifruit and its relatives (the genus Actinidia).

lore.who: New Zealand (the Auckland exporters Turners and Growers, 20th century)
lore.belief: The fruit grown from Chinese seed and sold as the 'Chinese gooseberry' was renamed kiwifruit, after the kiwi, the flightless bird found only in New Zealand and taken as its emblem; New Zealand servicemen were also known as 'Kiwis'. By 1969 the name was well established, and a vine from China had become a symbol of New Zealand.
lore.note: The review used here names the firm and the bird, but not the year the name was proposed.

history.who: Ancient Greece, Rome and medieval Europe
history.use: None: the fruit was unknown to them. It grows wild in the mountains of southwest China; the first botanical specimens reached Europe around the 1750s and the first fruits, preserved in spirit, reached Kew in London in 1886.
history.note: There is no Greek or Roman tradition to test. The fruit was domesticated only in the 20th century: seeds reached New Zealand in 1904, the Hayward variety spread from the late 1930s, and the old name 'Chinese gooseberry' gave way to 'kiwifruit' by 1969. Most varieties sold today are selections from wild plants, not bred over centuries.

history.who: China (Chinese pharmacopoeias from the Tang dynasty, AD 618–907, onwards)
history.use: The fruit, called mihoutao, was listed for aiding digestion, easing indigestion (dyspepsia) and vomiting, and reducing irritability.
history.note: Modern trials tested constipation rather than indigestion: two green kiwifruit a day gave somewhat more bowel movements, graded low by a 2025 guideline. A Zespri-funded review of 12 trials found smaller indigestion scores, but none tested indigestion as its main question. Irritability and vomiting haven't been tested.

history.who: Traditional medicine in China and East Asia (plants of the kiwifruit family, Actinidia)
history.use: Ten Actinidia species were used for digestive problems, rheumatism, kidney problems, heart and blood vessel problems, cancers, haemorrhoids and diabetes, among other illnesses. These uses are for the plants in general, often other parts than the fruit.
history.note: No trial of the eaten fruit has tested rheumatism, kidney disease, cancer, haemorrhoids or diabetes itself. Trials measured markers such as blood pressure, blood fats and blood sugar, which are only part of these questions.

sources.title: The genus Actinidia Lindl. (Actinidiaceae): A comprehensive review on its ethnobotany, phytochemistry, and pharmacological properties.

history.use: Its high vitamin C gave kiwifruit the name 'frutto della salute', the health fruit.
history.note: The vitamin C is real and reaches the blood: in trials, one to two kiwifruit a day raised low blood levels to what researchers call healthy or saturated. Whether that improves health beyond preventing a shortage is a separate question.

sources.title: The nutritional and health attributes of kiwifruit: a review.

inIt: Kiwifruit is best known for vitamin C. In the US food table, as quoted in a 2018 review, green Hayward kiwifruit has 92.7 mg per 100 g and SunGold 161.3 mg; green kiwifruit typically holds 80 to 120 mg, varying with growing region, harvest, storage and ripening.

The UK food table (CoFID) measures green kiwifruit flesh: per 100 g, 44 kcal, 8.3 g of sugars, 2.7 g of fibre, 71 mg of vitamin C, 289 mg of potassium, 2.17 mg of vitamin E and 33 µg of folate. It has no gold kiwifruit, and no vitamin K value for kiwifruit.

Its fibre includes soluble and insoluble kinds. A 2018 review reported that kiwifruit fibre swells and holds more water than wheat bran, sugar beet fibre or apple fibre, which is thought to matter for stool softness and transit. Two green kiwifruit of the size used in one large trial gave about 6 g of fibre.

Green kiwifruit contains actinidin, an enzyme that breaks down protein. It is the most abundant protein in kiwifruit and also its main allergen. SunGold has much less actinidin activity than green kiwifruit, and other gold varieties have none.

Other compounds include the carotenoids lutein, zeaxanthin and beta-carotene, chlorophylls, quinic acid, chlorogenic acid and other phenolic compounds. A sleep study describes serotonin in kiwifruit. The UK table measures none of these, nor actinidin, and a food has thousands of compounds no table tracks.
In the US table, green kiwifruit has 40.3 µg of vitamin K per 100 g and SunGold 6.1 µg, and green has 122 µg of lutein plus zeaxanthin per 100 g against 24 µg in SunGold.
processing: Green and gold are different fruits. In the US food table green Hayward has 3 g of fibre per 100 g against 1.4 g in SunGold, and 9.0 g of sugars against 12.3 g, and SunGold has 161.3 mg of vitamin C per 100 g against 92.7 mg. The UK table's kiwifruit (CoFID 14-371) is green, so its numbers don't describe gold kiwifruit.

Most trials used peeled fruit; in the largest constipation trial people were told to eat the kiwifruit without the skin. Eating SunGold with its skin adds about 50% more fibre, 32% more vitamin E and 34% more folate, according to the New Zealand food table quoted in a 2018 review. One small trial found the skin added some gut effects that the flesh alone didn't.

Actinidin, the protein-digesting enzyme, is strongest in green kiwifruit. In lab digestion models, green kiwifruit extract broke down proteins faster than SunGold extract, though SunGold did better for some proteins.

Heat and strong acid can change the structure of several kiwifruit allergens, a 2019 review reported; whether cooked kiwifruit is safe for people with kiwifruit allergy is a question for an allergist.

Kiwifruit capsules, powders and extracts (such as products sold for constipation) are a different product from the fruit. In meta-analyses they did not change stool frequency, while the whole fruit did.
whatStudiesDid: Constipation trials mostly gave two green kiwifruit a day for 4 weeks, peeled, compared with psyllium fibre (7.5 or 12 g a day) or prunes (100 g a day); one trial gave two gold kiwifruit a day. Blood pressure trials gave three kiwifruit a day for 8 weeks, compared with one apple a day or no change, or two kiwifruit before breakfast for 7 weeks. Vitamin C studies gave half to three gold kiwifruit a day for several weeks each. Mood and vitality trials gave two SunGold kiwifruit a day for 4 weeks. Sleep studies gave two kiwifruit an hour before bed for 4 weeks. Blood sugar studies gave kiwifruit before or with a starchy meal on single test days. An iron trial gave two gold kiwifruit with an iron-fortified breakfast cereal every day for 16 weeks.

findings.population: Adults with chronic constipation or constipation-type irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-C), in trials of the whole fruit, mostly two green kiwifruit a day for 4 weeks
whyThisGrade: The British Dietetic Association's 2025 guideline rated the evidence low using GRADE: kiwifruit gave more bowel movements than psyllium (high risk of bias, imprecision), and no difference was found in how many people had a clinical benefit
Neither participants nor kiwifruit could be blinded: everyone knew what they were eating
The largest trial (184 people) was mainly funded by Zespri, the New Zealand kiwifruit marketer, and two of its authors were Zespri employees; other trials also had Zespri support
Trials lasted 4 weeks; nothing is known about longer use
EFSA concluded that a cause and effect relationship is established for green Hayward kiwifruit and normal defecation, on an application from Zespri
findings.summary: In a 2024 meta-analysis, kiwifruit gave 0.36 more bowel movements a week than psyllium fibre (95% CI 0.24 to 0.48; 3 trials, 192 people), a small difference against a treatment that itself works; the 2025 British Dietetic Association guideline rated this low certainty and found no difference from psyllium in how many people had a clinical benefit (risk ratio 1.32, 0.91 to 1.92). A 2022 meta-analysis of 7 trials (399 people) found kiwifruit vs psyllium 1.01 more spontaneous bowel movements a week (−0.02 to 2.04). In the largest trial, in New Zealand, Italy and Japan, two green kiwifruit a day for 4 weeks raised complete spontaneous bowel movements by 1.53 a week in functional constipation and 1.73 in IBS-C, and improved gut comfort; psyllium's effect was clear only in IBS-C. In a US trial of 79 people, kiwifruit, prunes and psyllium all raised bowel movements; kiwifruit had the fewest side effects and the least dissatisfaction. Two gold kiwifruit a day worked about as well as psyllium in a smaller trial. Kiwifruit capsules and powders are a different product: in a 2023 meta-analysis of 3 trials they did not change stool frequency (0.24 a week, −0.32 to 0.80).
findings.bottomLine: In trials, two green kiwifruit a day for 4 weeks gave somewhat more bowel movements, slightly more than psyllium fibre and with few side effects. A 2025 guideline rated the evidence low, and kiwifruit capsules and powders did not show the same effect.
findings.label: Constipation
findings.line: Two green kiwifruit a day gave more bowel movements, slightly more than psyllium

findings.population: Adults, many with high-normal or raised blood pressure, in small randomised trials of the whole fruit (two or three a day)
whyThisGrade: Few trials: 6 in the 2026 meta-analysis and 5 in the 2019 one, which found no clear effect
In the best-measured trial, 24-hour blood pressure fell but office blood pressure didn't
The 2026 meta-analysis found larger effects in shorter trials (8 weeks or less) and asked for confirmation in larger trials
Unblinded designs (the comparison was an apple or no change)
findings.summary: A 2026 meta-analysis of 6 randomised trials (10 groups) found systolic blood pressure 5.73 mmHg lower (95% CI 2.44 to 9.02 lower) and diastolic 4.08 mmHg lower (2.10 to 6.07 lower) with kiwifruit, more with three a day, with raised starting blood pressure and in trials of 8 weeks or less; the authors asked for caution because there were few trials. A 2019 meta-analysis of 5 trials (489 people) found no clear effect: systolic −1.72 mmHg (−4.27 to 0.84), diastolic −2.35 (−5.10 to 0.41). In a Norwegian trial of 118 adults with high-normal or stage 1 high blood pressure, three kiwifruit a day for 8 weeks gave 24-hour systolic 3.6 mmHg (0.7 to 6.5) and diastolic 1.9 mmHg (0.3 to 3.6) lower than one apple a day, but office blood pressure did not differ. In 102 male smokers, three kiwifruit a day for 8 weeks lowered systolic by 10 and diastolic by 9 mmHg against controls. Two kiwifruit before breakfast for 7 weeks gave systolic 2.7 mmHg lower (0.0 to 5.5) in 42 healthy adults. No trial measured heart attacks or strokes.
findings.bottomLine: In small trials, two or three kiwifruit a day went with blood pressure a few mmHg lower, most in people whose pressure was raised. One meta-analysis found a clear effect and an older one didn't, and no trial measured heart attacks or strokes.
findings.label: Blood pressure
findings.line: A few mmHg lower in small trials, most when pressure was raised

findings.population: Adults, healthy or with heart risk factors, in small randomised trials of the whole fruit
whyThisGrade: Meta-analyses disagree: one found lower LDL, an older one found no effect on any blood fat
Few, small trials (5 to 6 per meta-analysis)
Several individual trials found no change in triglycerides or cholesterol
findings.summary: A 2024 meta-analysis of 6 randomised trials found LDL cholesterol 9.30 mg/dL lower with kiwifruit (95% CI 1.04 to 17.56 lower), but no clear change in triglycerides (−12.91 mg/dL, −28.17 to 2.34), total cholesterol or HDL. A 2019 meta-analysis of 5 trials (489 people) found no effect on LDL (−0.41 mmol/L, −0.99 to 0.18) or triglycerides (−0.23 mmol/L, −0.66 to 0.20). In a 2004 crossover trial in healthy volunteers, two or three kiwifruit a day for 28 days lowered triglycerides by 15% compared with control, with no change in cholesterol. Two kiwifruit a day for 7 weeks (42 people) and two SunGold a day for 6 weeks (23 people) did not change triglycerides or cholesterol.
findings.bottomLine: Results on blood fats disagree. One meta-analysis found LDL cholesterol slightly lower with kiwifruit, another found no effect, and several small trials found no change in triglycerides or cholesterol.

findings.outcome: Blood sugar after a starchy meal
findings.population: Healthy adults on single test days, with kiwifruit eaten before or with cereal or rice
whyThisGrade: Small crossover studies (9 to 30 people), all in healthy adults, from one research group in New Zealand
Single test meals: they show the response to one meal, not long-term blood sugar
In longer trials fasting blood sugar didn't change, and no trial tested people with diabetes
findings.summary: In 30 healthy Chinese adults, eating kiwifruit before a rice meal (replacing part of the rice) gave a blood sugar peak 0.9 mmol/L lower at breakfast (95% CI 0.2 to 1.6) and 1.1 mmol/L lower at lunch (0.5 to 1.7) than the rice meal eaten at one sitting. In 9 healthy adults, whole kiwifruit pulp eaten with wheat cereal almost halved the rise in blood sugar compared with a meal with the same sugars added, and avoided a later dip; fibre and organic acids each explained part of it. A 2017 study in 20 people found similar results. Over weeks, kiwifruit did not change fasting blood sugar: 0.09 mmol/L (−0.06 to 0.24) after 7 weeks in 42 people, and no clear change in a 2024 meta-analysis.
findings.bottomLine: In small studies in healthy adults, kiwifruit eaten with or instead of part of a starchy meal gave a lower blood sugar peak after that meal. Over weeks it didn't change fasting blood sugar, and people with diabetes weren't tested.
findings.label: Blood sugar after a starchy meal
findings.line: Lower peak after that meal in small studies in healthy adults

findings.population: Young adults and others with low or below-average vitamin C levels, eating gold kiwifruit
whyThisGrade: Consistent across several studies, with a large effect on a nutrient the fruit is measured to contain
But small: 14 to 167 people, and the dose study had no control group and gave doses in a fixed order
Zespri funded or co-funded most of these studies
A blood level, not a health outcome
findings.summary: In 15 young men with below-average vitamin C, gold kiwifruit (about 80 mg of vitamin C each) raised plasma vitamin C from 38 µmol/L to 50 with half a kiwifruit a day, 53 with one and 62 with two; three a day reached 68 at first, then 58. Urine vitamin C rose from two a day, suggesting the blood was close to saturated. Four weeks after stopping it was back to 42. In a trial of 167 young adults with low vitamin C, two SunGold a day brought plasma vitamin C to saturation within two weeks, as did a 250 mg tablet. In 20 adults with a history of severe respiratory infections, two SunGold a day for six weeks raised vitamin C above 60 µmol/L, but about one in five didn't reach 50, possibly because of smoking or higher body weight.
findings.bottomLine: In small studies, one to two gold kiwifruit a day raised low blood vitamin C to levels researchers call healthy or saturated, much as a vitamin C tablet did. Smokers and heavier people rose less, and the studies measured blood levels, not health.
findings.label: Vitamin C in the blood
findings.line: Raised low levels much as a vitamin C tablet did, in small studies

findings.population: Young adults with low vitamin C, and adults with mild to moderate mood disturbance, eating two SunGold kiwifruit a day
whyThisGrade: Two small trials; the larger was reanalysed after a published comment that it mixed random and non-random allocation, and its corrected title no longer calls it randomised
Self-reported mood: the kiwifruit groups knew what they were eating (the comparison was a tablet or usual diet)
The larger trial was funded by Zespri
Results weakened when adjusted for other factors in the smartphone analysis
findings.summary: In a trial of 167 young adults with low vitamin C, two SunGold kiwifruit a day for 4 weeks lowered fatigue and improved well-being after two weeks compared with placebo, with a trend for mood; a 250 mg vitamin C tablet improved well-being, and mood and fatigue only in those with consistently low vitamin C. A later analysis of daily smartphone surveys found kiwifruit improved vitality and mood within days, but the effects weakened after adjusting for other factors. A published comment said the trial mixed random and non-random allocation, and a correction removed 'randomized' from its title. In a 2025 crossover trial of 26 adults with mild to moderate mood disturbance, without blinding, four weeks of two SunGold a day lowered mood disturbance scores by 65% compared with usual diet.
findings.bottomLine: Two small trials found better self-reported mood and vitality with two gold kiwifruit a day. People knew they were eating kiwifruit, one trial's randomisation was questioned, and the evidence is very weak.
findings.label: Mood and vitality
findings.line: Better self-reported mood in two small trials; very weak evidence

findings.population: Adults with self-reported sleep problems, elite athletes and students with insomnia symptoms, eating two kiwifruit an hour before bed
whyThisGrade: The two studies with good news had no control group (24 adults; 15 athletes), so expectation and time could explain the changes
The athletes' study used only questionnaires and diaries
The only controlled trial found (74 students, kiwifruit vs pear) found no difference in sleep measured by a wrist device; it isn't in Europe PMC and was read only as described in a later paper
findings.summary: In a 2011 study without a control group, 24 adults in Taiwan with sleep problems ate two kiwifruit an hour before bed for 4 weeks; total sleep time measured by a wrist device rose by 13.4% and sleep efficiency by 5.41%, and time to fall asleep fell by 35.4%. In 15 elite athletes, also without a control group, the same amount for 4 weeks went with better sleep quality scores and longer self-reported sleep. In a 2017 trial in 74 students with insomnia symptoms, 130 g of kiwifruit or of pear an hour before bed for 4 weeks gave no difference in sleep measured by a wrist device, though the kiwifruit group rated their sleep quality and daytime function better (as described in the athletes' paper).
findings.bottomLine: Studies without a control group found longer sleep after two kiwifruit before bed, but the one controlled trial, against pear, found no difference in sleep measured by a wrist device. The evidence is very weak.
findings.label: Sleep
findings.line: Longer sleep in uncontrolled studies, no difference in the one controlled trial

findings.outcome: Iron status with an iron-fortified breakfast
findings.population: Women aged 18 to 44 with low iron stores (ferritin 25 µg/L or less), in New Zealand
whyThisGrade: A single randomised trial
The kiwifruit was eaten with a cereal fortified with iron; it isn't known whether the effect holds for other meals
20 of 89 women weren't in the final analysis
Unblinded (kiwifruit vs banana); the abstract doesn't say who funded it
findings.summary: In a 16-week trial, 89 women with low iron stores ate an iron-fortified breakfast cereal (16 mg of iron) with milk and either two gold kiwifruit (164 mg of vitamin C) or one banana every day. In the 69 analysed, median ferritin rose by 10.0 µg/L in the kiwifruit group against 1.0 µg/L in the banana group, and soluble transferrin receptor, another iron marker, fell more. The authors linked it to the vitamin C and the carotenoids lutein and zeaxanthin, which can help iron absorption.
findings.bottomLine: In one trial in women with low iron stores, two gold kiwifruit eaten with an iron-fortified breakfast cereal raised ferritin more than a banana did over 16 weeks. It is a single trial, tied to a fortified meal.
findings.label: Iron with a fortified breakfast
findings.line: Ferritin rose more than with a banana in one trial in women with low iron

steps.label: Fibre that holds water
steps.text: Kiwifruit fibre swells and holds more water than wheat bran, sugar beet or apple fibre, a 2018 review reported. Two green kiwifruit gave about 6 g of fibre in a large trial.

steps.label: More water in the bowel
steps.text: In an MRI study of 14 healthy adults, two kiwifruit twice a day for 3 days left more water in the small bowel and a larger colon than a control drink, with 1.46 vs 1.14 stools a day and softer stools.

steps.label: Gut bacteria ferment it
steps.text: Bacteria in the colon ferment kiwifruit fibre, which the review lists as another likely part of the effect, with changes in the bacteria and what they make.

steps.label: Actinidin breaks down protein
steps.text: Green kiwifruit holds actinidin, an enzyme that broke down proteins faster in lab digestion models, more with green than with SunGold. Whether this helps digestion in people isn't known.

whoShouldBeCareful.with: Kiwifruit allergy, or allergy to latex or some pollens
whoShouldBeCareful.note: Kiwifruit allergy was first described in 1981 and ranges from itching and swelling in the mouth (oral allergy syndrome) to life-threatening anaphylaxis. It can cross-react with latex, pollens and other fruits, and severe reactions were reported more often in children than in adults. Actinidin, the enzyme in green kiwifruit, is its main allergen. Trials left out people with kiwifruit or latex allergy. If you react to kiwifruit, latex or pollen, talk to your doctor or an allergist.

Two trials found kiwifruit lowered how readily platelets clump in lab tests of blood: by 18% with two or three a day for 28 days in healthy volunteers, and by 15% with three a day for 8 weeks in male smokers. No study tested people taking blood thinners, and none showed bleeding, so the evidence for an interaction is weak and indirect. Kiwifruit also contains vitamin K (40.3 µg per 100 g in green, 6.1 µg in SunGold, US food table), which the UK table doesn't measure. If you take a blood thinner, talk to your doctor before eating much more kiwifruit than usual.

The UK food table lists 289 mg of potassium per 100 g of green kiwifruit. The constipation trials left out people with significant kidney disease. If you have been told to limit potassium, talk to your doctor or renal dietitian about kiwifruit.

cautions: In trials kiwifruit caused few side effects: in the US trial, side effects were least common with kiwifruit and most common with psyllium, and the largest trial reported no significant adverse events. Kiwifruit capsule extracts may have more minor side effects than placebo (risk ratio 4.58, 95% CI 0.79 to 26.4), which could be chance.
Kiwifruit is not a treatment for high blood pressure, iron deficiency or sleep problems. Anything clearly out of range in your results is worth discussing with your doctor.
unknowns: Most trials lasted 4 to 8 weeks. Nothing is known about effects over years, and no trial measured heart attacks, strokes or deaths.
Much of the research was funded by Zespri, which markets New Zealand kiwifruit, or done by researchers with ties to it; several abstracts don't say who paid. Independent trials are fewer.
Green and gold kiwifruit differ in fibre, vitamin C, actinidin and vitamin K, and trials used different kinds, so a result for one kind may not hold for the other.

It isn't known which parts of the fruit explain the gut effects: fibre, actinidin, other compounds, or all together. The UK table measures fibre and vitamin C but not actinidin, carotenoids or other compounds, and a food has thousands of compounds no table tracks.
Sleep has been tested mostly without control groups; the only controlled trial found didn't show a difference in measured sleep.
Kiwifruit capsules, powders and extracts are a different product; trials of them don't show what the fruit does, and the fruit's trials don't show what they do.
